theme: The 144,000 on Mount Zion; the harvest; the bowls
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 14:1-15:8. Chapter 14 shows a series of visions of the Lamb and his people, followed by announcements of judgment. Chapter 15 introduces the final seven plagues, with the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Notice the contrast between the Lamb’s people on Mount Zion and the world under the beast.
settingTheScene: After the dragon and the beasts, the book gives a series of contrasts to encourage the persecuted church. Where the beast’s followers have its mark on their foreheads, the Lamb’s followers have his name and his Father’s name. These chapters sit between the unveiling of the evil powers and the final outpouring of God’s wrath. They announce the fall of Babylon, the final harvest, and the song that celebrates God’s justice. Some interpreters see these scenes as parallel to previous ones, returning to the same period from another angle; others see them as moving forward in a chronological sequence.
observation: “On Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads” (14:1).
“It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (14:4).
“Another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people” (14:6).
“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on” (14:13).
“One like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand” (14:14).
“The song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (15:3).
“All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed” (15:4).
interpretation:
John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who have the name of the Lamb and his Father written on their foreheads. This contrasts with the mark of the beast. A sound from heaven like many waters and loud thunder, and like harpists playing on their harps, accompanies a new song before the throne. The 144,000 are described as those who have not defiled themselves with women (probably a figurative way of saying they have kept themselves pure from the spiritual adultery of idolatry), who “follow the Lamb wherever he goes,” and who were redeemed as firstfruits for God and the Lamb. “In their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.” As in chapter 7, they are the whole redeemed people seen as a purified army.

Then three angels. The first flies in midheaven with “an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and the earth.” Even in these final scenes, the gospel is proclaimed to every nation. The second angel announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” the first mention of the city that will be described fully in chapters 17 and 18. The third warns that anyone who worships the beast will drink the wine of God’s wrath and be tormented, with no rest day or night. Then a call: “Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.” A voice from heaven says, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Blessed indeed,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!” This is among the most comforting verses in the book for those who grieve: those who die in Christ are blessed.

Next come two images of harvest. One like a son of man on a white cloud with a sharp sickle reaps the earth’s harvest, which is ripe. An angel then gathers the vintage of the earth and throws it into the great winepress of the wrath of God, and blood flows to a horse’s bridle for 1,600 stadia. These images of judgment are drawn from Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1-6. Interpreters differ on whether the first harvest is the gathering of the righteous (as grain) and the second is the judgment (as grapes), or whether both refer to judgment. What is clear is that the Lord of the harvest has the final say.

Chapter 15 introduces “another sign in heaven, great and amazing: seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.” John sees those who had conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mingled with fire, with harps of God in their hands. They sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”: “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.” Like Israel after the Red Sea (Exodus 15), the redeemed sing on the shore after their deliverance. The song combines the two great redemptions: the exodus and the cross. Then the temple is opened, and the seven angels come out dressed in pure bright linen, and one of the four living creatures gives them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath. The temple fills with smoke from God’s glory and power, and none can enter until the plagues are completed.
connection: Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1-6 are the images of harvest and winepress. Exodus 15:1-18 is the song of Moses. Deuteronomy 32 is another song of Moses. Psalm 86:9-10 and 98:1-3 speak of the nations worshiping. Isaiah 21:9 and Jeremiah 51:8 announce the fall of Babylon. Matthew 13:24-43 describes the harvest at the end of the age. Matthew 24:14 says the gospel will be preached to all nations. Hebrews 4:9-11 speaks of rest. 1 Corinthians 15:58 says our labor is not in vain. Exodus 40:34-35 and 1 Kings 8:10-11 show the glory filling the temple.
application:
Remember, when you grieve a believer who has died, that their deeds follow them and they rest from their labors (14:13).

Ask whom you can tell the “eternal gospel,” and pray for opportunity this week.

Sing a song of deliverance today, and use the words of 15:3-4.
prayerPrompts: Praise God that great and amazing are his deeds.
Ask him to give you a heart that fears and glorifies him.
Thank him for those who endure.
